Daniel’s proposal leans on an analogy to Bitcoin’s “51% attack” that doesn’t translate cleanly to Tor, and that mismatch hides the key difficulty: Tor nodes are not a stable, identity-weighted electorate but a permissionless set of relays where influence is cheap to manufacture. Any “>50% of nodes” mechanism is structurally vulnerable to Sybil capture—one actor (including the very state agencies that might want broader surveillance powers) can spin up many relays and thereby “vote” content off the network without representing anything like majority public will, a problem long formalized in the literature as the [Sybil attack](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/646334.687813). Daniel gestures at this with “Every person is equal; not every Tor node,” but that’s not a footnote—it’s the crux: once you try to weight votes by something harder to fake (identity, stake, reputation, geography), you reintroduce centralization and gatekeeping, i.e., the very thing Tor was built to route around.

There’s also a more basic technical blind spot: “expose a specific hidden service” is not a localized operation that the network can perform on command without redesigning onion services into something like key escrow or a built‑in tracing backdoor. Relays generally do not *know* which onion service a given circuit ultimately supports, and onion services are designed specifically so that no single relay learns both “who” and “where” ([Tor onion services overview](https://community.torproject.org/onion-services/); classic design goals in the [Tor design paper](https://svn.torproject.org/svn/projects/design-paper/tor-design.html.en)). To add a protocol feature that makes deanonymization possible *when a quorum agrees* is to add a feature that makes deanonymization possible *in principle*—and then the real question becomes who gets to define “unwanted,” how that definition changes under pressure, and how often “quorum” quietly becomes “whoever has the budget to run enough relays.” That isn’t a slippery-slope rhetorical move; it’s a direct consequence of building enforcement into the routing layer.

If Daniel’s goal is specifically to reduce child sexual abuse material, the most promising directions tend to sit outside “Tor votes to unmask”: targeted investigation of operators (opsec mistakes, payment trails, infiltration), exploitation of server-side vulnerabilities, and disruption of hosting and infrastructure when the underlying machines are found—tactics that have, in practice, led to takedowns without requiring Tor to become a content-moderation system. The post would be stronger if it separated *moral consensus* (“most people want this gone”) from *network governance* (how decisions are made under adversarial conditions) and from *protocol capability* (what information relays can even access), because conflating those three is exactly how well-intended “safety” features become general-purpose censorship or surveillance primitives.
